title: Round Hill is suing Suno and Anthropic for up to $1B apiece. It isn’t looking to settle.

reading.body:
The core failure here is a data-sourcing decision made before deployment. Suno admitted its model was trained on essentially all music files on the internet, and reporting based on a hack indicated that sources included YouTube, Deezer, and Genius. No licensing or rights-clearance step was built into that pipeline. The failure is not in the model's inference behavior alone but in the training data acquisition practice that preceded any public release.

The downstream consequence is that the deployed system can reproduce outputs that closely replicate specific copyrighted recordings. Record labels demonstrated this by using targeted prompts to generate music nearly identical to identified commercial tracks. That is a model asserting, through its outputs, a competence built on material it had no documented right to use. A rights-clearance audit of training data, or a filtering step to exclude identified copyrighted works, would have been the point at which this could have been caught before deployment.

What is not established: the lawsuits and class actions are allegations and legal proceedings, not findings of liability, and while a German court ruled against Suno in the GEMA case and some parties reached settlements, the broader US litigation and its outcomes remain unresolved. Allegations of deliberate concealment of training sources are claims made in pleadings, not proven facts.

summary:
Major record labels, including Universal Music Group, Sony Music, Warner Music, and others, have filed separate lawsuits against Udio and Suno, two popular artificial intelligence music generators. The labels accuse both companies of scraping massive amounts of copyrighted music without permission or compensation to train their AI models. The lawsuits claim that these companies not only illegally used existing recordings but also directly reproduce sections of famous songs in their generated music. The record labels argue that Udio and Suno have been deliberately unclear about what content they copied and that admitting the truth would reveal widespread copyright infringement.

As part of the lawsuits, the record labels submitted thousands of copyrighted works they claim were used for training, including music from The Beatles, Michael Jackson, Bruce Springsteen, and many others. The labels demonstrated their case by using specific prompts to generate songs that closely replicate famous recordings, including near-identical versions of Green Day's American Idiot and Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas Is You. The companies previously claimed their use of copyrighted material constituted fair use. Udio was sued in New York, while Suno was sued in Massachusetts, and these cases are expected to set important precedents for how generative AI services can legally use existing creative works.
